questions.question: What must a function $\pi:A\to A$ do in order to be a permutation of $A$?
options: It must be strictly increasing.
It must be defined only on one element.
It must be bijective.
It must send $A$ into a larger set.

questions.question: What does a permutation do to the elements of a finite set?
options: It changes the size of the set.
It deletes one element and repeats another.
It sends every element to the same image.
It rearranges them without loss or duplication.

questions.question: Why must the codomain of a permutation of $A$ be $A$ itself?
options: The codomain has to be empty.
The codomain must have twice as many elements.
A permutation must always map into $\mathbb R$.
It rearranges one set, not mapping into a different set.

questions.question: What happens when two permutations of the same set are composed?
options: The result is defined only for finite sets with two elements.
The result maps into a different set.
The result is again a permutation of that set.
The result is never bijective.

questions.question: How many permutations does a finite set with $n$ elements have?
How many permutations does the set $\{1,2,3\}$ have?
Which map on $\{1,2,3\}$ is a permutation?
options: $1\mapsto2$, $2\mapsto3$, $3\mapsto1$.
$1\mapsto4$, $2\mapsto1$, $3\mapsto2$.
$1\mapsto2$, $2\mapsto2$, $3\mapsto3$.
$1\mapsto1$, $2\mapsto1$, $3\mapsto2$.

questions.question: The map on $\{a,b,c\}$ that swaps $a$ and $b$ and leaves $c$ fixed sends $a$ where?
options: Outside the set.

questions.question: How many permutations does a set with $4$ elements have?
Why is $f(1)=2$, $f(2)=2$, $f(3)=3$ not a permutation of $\{1,2,3\}$?
options: The image $2$ is too large.
Two inputs share an image, so it is not injective.
The domain and codomain are different sets.
The map has too many images.

questions.question: Why does every permutation have an inverse permutation?
options: Every function has an inverse function.
A bijection reverses to another bijection $A\to A$.
The inverse is obtained by deleting fixed points.
The inverse exists only if the set is infinite.

questions.question: What is a fixed point of a permutation?
options: An element that is deleted by the permutation.
An element that is not in the domain.
An element that has two images.
An element that is mapped to itself.

questions.question: Why is a map that is injective but not onto not a permutation?
options: A permutation must fail injectivity.
Only constant maps are permutations.
A permutation must be both injective and surjective.
Surjectivity is forbidden for permutations.

questions.question: Let $\pi$ on $\{1,2,3\}$ be given by $\pi(1)=2$, $\pi(2)=3$, $\pi(3)=1$. What is $\pi^2(1)$?
options: Undefined.

questions.question: For the swap of $1$ and $2$ in $\{1,2,3\}$, what is the inverse permutation?
options: No inverse exists.
The constant map to $1$.
The cycle $1\mapsto2\mapsto3\mapsto1$.
The same swap again.

questions.question: If $\pi=(1\ 2\ 3)$ sends $1\to2$, $2\to3$, $3\to1$, what is $\pi^{-1}(1)$?
options: No such element.

questions.question: Why do permutations of a set form a natural system under composition?
options: The codomain changes after each composition.
They are closed under composition and each has an inverse.
Permutations are not functions.
Composition turns every permutation into a constant map.

questions.question: A rearrangement of a finite list repeats one element and omits another. Why is it not a permutation?
options: Not bijective: duplicate and omission.
It can be written using arrows.
It maps the set to itself.
It has too many fixed points.

questions.question: Let $\pi(1)=3$, $\pi(2)=1$, $\pi(3)=2$. What is $\pi^3(1)$?
options: Undefined.

questions.question: A permutation of $\{1,2,3,4\}$ fixes $1$ and swaps $2$ and $4$, while $3$ is fixed. How many elements are moved?
